slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L

What it is used for: This value is part of the blood differential, which measures the amount and/or percentage of each type of white blood cell. Because the five types do different jobs, measuring them separately gives important information. The test is ordered at routine checkups, to find the cause of symptoms (such as unusual tiredness, weakness or unexplained bruising) or of an abnormal WBC count on another test, and to monitor an existing blood disorder; it helps diagnose infections, autoimmune diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis, leukemia and other cancers.

Physiology: Neutrophils are the most common type of white blood cell and the body’s main defense against infection when bacteria, viruses or other germs enter the body; they mostly target bacterial infections.

slides.title: Neutrophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: A higher-than-normal amount of neutrophils is known as neutrophilia.
Low: A lower-than-normal amount of neutrophils is known as neutropenia.

Low: Some cancers and treatments such as chemotherapy lower white cell counts and raise infection risk: at times in the treatment cycle neutrophils are particularly low. Blood tests check for neutropenia during treatment; signs of infection (such as a fever of 38 °C or higher) need urgent care.

slides.title: Neutrophils, Monocytes, Eosinophils, Basophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood differential.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.
Interferences: Blood differential results can be affected by physical injury or extreme stress, smoking and alcohol use; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
Limitations: If results seem abnormal, the provider may order other tests to find the cause; symptoms, medical history and other blood test results are considered.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L

Physiology: Lymphocytes include two main types: B cells and T cells. B cells fight off invading viruses, bacteria or toxins; certain T cells target and destroy the body’s own cells, such as cancer cells and virus-infected cells.
Lymphocytes mostly target viral infections.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: A higher-than-normal amount of lymphocytes is known as lymphocytosis.
Low: A lower-than-normal amount of lymphocytes is known as lymphopenia.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for a blood differential.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.
Interferences: Blood differential results can be affected by physical injury or extreme stress, smoking and alcohol use; an abnormal result does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.
Limitations: CD4 cells (“helper T cells”) are a type of lymphocyte that HIV attacks and destroys. A separate test — the CD4 count — is used to check the immune system in people with HIV.

slides.title: Lymphocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: If results seem abnormal, the provider may order other tests to find the cause; symptoms, medical history and other blood test results are considered.

slides.title: Monocytes
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Monocytes kill bacteria, viruses and other germs that may cause illness. They also boost the body’s immune response and clear away dead cells.

slides.title: Eosinophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Eosinophils defend against parasites and infections, are involved in allergies and help control inflammation (swelling and redness).

Normally the blood does not have a large number of eosinophils. In some conditions they move out of the bloodstream and build up in organs and tissues such as the esophagus, heart, lungs and intestines, causing inflammation.

slides.title: Eosinophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: The body may produce more eosinophils in response to allergic disorders, skin conditions, parasitic and fungal infections, autoimmune diseases, some cancers and bone marrow disorders.

slides.title: Basophils
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: %, ×10⁹/L
Physiology: Basophils release enzymes during allergic reactions and asthma attacks.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous or fingertip capillary blood; heel stick in babies

What it is used for: For a blood smear, blood is spread on a glass slide and treated with a special stain; a laboratory professional then checks the size, shape and number of red cells, white cells and platelets under a microscope. Automatic computer programs may be used to help.

A blood smear alone can't diagnose a disease, but with other tests it helps diagnose and monitor blood and bone marrow disorders, certain cancers of the blood, bone marrow and lymphatic system, infections and certain parasites.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: After an abnormal CBC, a smear confirms cell size and number and shows more about how the cells look, including their color. It is also ordered for symptoms of a blood-cell condition (fatigue, jaundice, unusual bleeding, easy bruising, fever, bone pain, swollen lymph nodes), to check treatment of anemia or blood cancer, and for flu-like symptoms in people living in or travelling to areas where malaria or babesiosis is common.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Results describe what the cells look like and how many there are, and anything else unusual, such as parasites. Abnormal red cells may be a sign of anemia, sickle cell disease, hemolytic anemia, thalassemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal white cells of infection, leukemia or bone marrow disorders; abnormal platelets of thrombocytopenia, thrombocytosis or thrombocythemia.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, though fasting may be required if other tests are ordered. Blood is drawn from a vein, sometimes by finger prick, and from the heel in babies.
Interferences: Severe illness, stress and blood transfusions can also cause abnormal smear results.
Limitations: Smear results alone usually can't diagnose a condition: the provider combines them with history, symptoms and other tests and may order more tests to find the cause.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10⁹/L, /µL

What it is used for: The test helps diagnose or monitor disorders with a high or low WBC: signs of infection (fever, chills, body aches, headache, a wound that is red, has pus or won’t heal, an ongoing cough), inflammation or autoimmune disease; and a disease or medicine that weakens the immune system — if the count gets too low, the provider may adjust treatment. Children may be tested as part of routine screening.

Physiology: White blood cells (leukocytes) are part of the immune system: made in the bone marrow and found in the blood and lymph tissue, they travel through the bloodstream and tissues to where they are needed to fight infections and other diseases. There are five major types — neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils and basophils; the WBC measures their total number.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: When you get sick, the body makes more white cells to fight bacteria, viruses or other foreign substances, raising the count. Some cancers, HIV (a virus that attacks white cells) and certain medicines such as chemotherapy lower it.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
bullets: High: Causes of leukocytosis (a high WBC) include infection, an inflammatory disease such as rheumatoid arthritis, allergy, leukemia or Hodgkin disease, and tissue damage from a burn or surgery. Smoking, stress, a reaction to a medicine or pregnancy can also raise the count.

Low: Causes of leukopenia (a low WBC) include bone marrow damage from infection, disease or treatments such as chemotherapy, cancers that affect the bone marrow, an autoimmune disorder such as lupus, and HIV.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/2
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed, but some medicines may need to be stopped before the test, so tell the provider about everything you take. Do not stop any medicine unless the provider says so.
Adults give a sample from a vein. Newborns and young babies have a heel stick; older babies and children give blood from the fingertip or arm.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: White blood cell count (WBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/2
bullets: Limitations: A WBC shows whether white cells are too high or too low but cannot confirm a diagnosis; it is usually done with a complete blood count, blood differential, blood smear and/or bone marrow test. The differential shows the amount of each type.

slides.title: Segmented neutrophil
slides.caption:
Size: 12–15 µm
Nucleus: 2–5 lobes joined by thin chromatin strands; deep purple
Cytoplasm: Abundant, pale pink
Granules: Very small, numerous, mauve
Key feature: Thin “thread” between lobes — that makes it segmented.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Band neutrophil
slides.caption:
Size: Not given separately (immature granulocytes: 12–18 µm)
Nucleus: Not divided into lobes: an elongated, curved band (C or S shape)
Cytoplasm: Pale pink, as in a segmented neutrophil
Granules: Fine, mauve
Key feature: No lobes separated by a thin strand.
Seen in: Increased in infections and myelodysplasia; in Pelger–Huët anomaly nuclear shape is altered congenitally.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Small lymphocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 7–10 µm
Nucleus: Round, fills most of the cell; dense, dark chromatin
Cytoplasm: Scant — a thin blue rim
Granules: None
Key feature: A little larger than a red cell, almost all nucleus.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Large lymphocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 10–15 µm
Nucleus: Round or oval, may lie to one side
Cytoplasm: More abundant, clear pale blue
Granules: May have a few large dark-red (azurophilic) granules
Key feature: Clear blue cytoplasm, no vacuoles or dust-like granules.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Monocyte
slides.caption:
Size: 15–25 µm — the largest leukocyte
Nucleus: Variable, often kidney-shaped; pale chromatin in strands
Cytoplasm: Grey-blue; vacuoles usually present
Granules: Fine, dust-like, reddish
Key feature: Large + pale folded nucleus + grey “ground-glass” cytoplasm.
Seen in: In malaria, brown-black pigment may be seen in the cytoplasm.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Eosinophil
slides.caption:
Size: 12–15 µm
Nucleus: Usually 2 lobes (“spectacles”)
Cytoplasm: Barely visible because of the granules
Granules: Large, round, densely packed, orange-red
Key feature: Large orange-red granules — no other cell has this colour.
Seen in: Sometimes the cell is damaged with scattered granules.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Basophil
slides.caption:
Size: 11–13 µm
Nucleus: Hard to see — covered by granules
Cytoplasm: Barely visible; sometimes small colourless vacuoles
Granules: Very large, deep purple; less densely packed than in eosinophils
Key feature: The rarest granulocyte; granules cover the nucleus too.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Reactive (atypical) lymphocyte
slides.caption:
Size: Very variable, 12–18 µm
Nucleus: Round or irregular, often to one side; nucleoli may be seen
Cytoplasm: Darker blue than a large lymphocyte; dark edge
Granules: None
Key feature: Blue cytoplasm darkening towards the edge, no granules.
Seen in: Viral infections (especially infectious mononucleosis), whooping cough, measles; tuberculosis, severe malaria, AIDS.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Neutrophil with toxic granulation
slides.caption:
Size: Neutrophil-sized
Nucleus: Neutrophil nucleus: lobes or band visible
Cytoplasm: Pale pink or pale blue
Granules: Very large and darkly stained
Key feature: It is a neutrophil — count it as one; note the toxic granulation separately.
Seen in: Seen with immature granulocytes in severe bacterial infections. Analysers cannot report it — only the smear shows it.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Hypersegmented neutrophil
slides.caption:
Size: Often larger than a normal neutrophil
Nucleus: 5–10 lobes
Cytoplasm: As in a normal neutrophil
Granules: Fine, mauve
Key feature: Count the lobes: 5 or more.
Seen in: Macrocytic anaemia from folate or vitamin B12 deficiency.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Blast
slides.caption:
Refer to a physician / haematologist
Size: Large, 15–25 µm (lymphoblast)
Nucleus: Large, round, pale, fine chromatin; 1–5 nucleoli
Cytoplasm: Narrow dark-blue rim, clear zone around the nucleus
Granules: None
Key feature: Nucleoli + fine chromatin + very little cytoplasm.
Seen in: A blast is an immature blood cell; seen in blood films in leukaemia.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Smudge (basket) cell
slides.caption:
Size: No clear outline
Nucleus: A smeared remnant of the nucleus
Cytoplasm: Absent
Granules: None
Key feature: A remnant of a broken leukocyte, not a separate cell type.
Seen in: Seen in both reactive and malignant lymphocytosis; not diagnostic of CLL on their own. How to record them follows your laboratory’s procedure.
Schematic (not a photomicrograph)

slides.title: Left shift
bullets: A higher share of band and younger granulocytes. On an analyser, “left shift” is a qualitative flag: a signal to scan the smear and do a manual differential if needed.
Severe bacterial infections (immature granulocytes enter the blood)
Infections; myelodysplasia (altered nuclear shape)
In leukopenia, even a relative rise in bands is given weight in a sepsis work-up

slides.title: Neutrophilia
bullets: Increased proportion or number of neutrophils.
Acute infection (most common), inflammation
Acute stress, trauma
Rheumatoid arthritis, rheumatic fever, thyroiditis, gout, eclampsia
Acute or chronic leukaemia, myeloproliferative diseases
Cigarette smoking

slides.title: Neutropenia
bullets: A lower-than-normal number of neutrophils in the blood.
Severe widespread bacterial infection (sepsis)
Influenza and other viral infections
Chemotherapy, radiation exposure
Aplastic anaemia

slides.title: Lymphocytosis
bullets: Increased proportion or number of lymphocytes. In children a lymphocyte majority can be age-related — use age-specific references.
Viral infections (measles, mumps), infectious mononucleosis, infectious hepatitis
Chronic infections: tuberculosis, malaria, chronic bacterial infection
Lymphocytic leukaemia, multiple myeloma

slides.title: Lymphopenia
bullets: A lower-than-normal number of lymphocytes in the blood.
HIV/AIDS
Chemotherapy, radiation, steroid use
Sepsis, leukaemia; ageing

slides.title: Eosinophilia
bullets: Increased eosinophils; often a response to infection or allergens.
Tissue parasites (schistosomiasis, filariasis, hookworm, ascariasis)
Allergic reactions
Addison disease, collagen vascular disease
Chronic myelogenous leukaemia, hypereosinophilic syndromes, cancer

slides.title: Monocytosis
bullets: Increased proportion or number of monocytes.
Tuberculosis, typhoid fever
Parasitic: malaria, visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar)
Viral: mononucleosis, mumps, measles
Chronic inflammatory disease, leukaemia

slides.title: Basophilia
bullets: Increased basophils. Basophils are the rarest granulocyte; judge by the absolute count rather than the percentage.
Chronic myelogenous leukaemia, myeloproliferative diseases
Allergic reactions
After splenectomy; chickenpox; collagen vascular disease

slides.title: Collecting the blood
bullets: From the side of the third or fourth finger; let the blood flow freely.
Not from the index finger, thumb, an infected finger or the ear (ear blood has too many monocytes).
If the film cannot be made within 1–2 hours, use EDTA (K₂). Heparin alters leukocytes and platelets — do not use it.

slides.title: Making the film
bullets: 1. Put a drop of about 4 mm diameter on a clean, grease-free slide.
2. Place the smooth-edged spreader in front of the drop and draw it back to touch the drop.
3. Let the blood run along the spreader edge.
4. Push to the end in one smooth movement — the blood should be used up before the end. Spread faster for anaemic blood.
5. Air-dry; label with a pencil on the thick part.

slides.title: A good film
bullets: No lines across or along the film.
A smooth end, not ragged.
Neither too long nor too thick.
No holes (a sign of a greasy slide).
A badly spread film gives a wrong differential.

slides.title: Fixing and staining (May–Grünwald + Giemsa)
bullets: 1. Fix with methanol for 2–3 minutes.
2. May–Grünwald 1 in 2 (buffered water) — 5 minutes.
3. Tip off and cover with Giemsa 1 in 10 — 10 minutes. Mix gently: shaking makes it precipitate.
4. Wash the stain off with a stream of buffered water — do not tip it off (leaves deposit).
5. Leave clean water for 2–3 minutes to differentiate, pH 6.8–7.0; then dry.
6. Prepare diluted stains for one day only; a new batch may need adjusted times.

slides.title: Where and how to count
bullets: With the ×100 oil objective, first check leukocytes are evenly spread: in a bad film neutrophils collect at the end.
Count in the readable monolayer just before the thin end: red cells touch but do not overlap. Avoid the thick part and the very edge.
Move field to field systematically in one direction without going back, so no cell is counted twice. Digital morphology analysers also scan in a “battlement” track.
Usually 100 leukocytes are counted. With very low or high counts some laboratories count from 25 up to 200–300 — follow your SOP.
Absolute count = fraction × total WBC. It reflects the true increase or decrease.

slides.title: Moving along the film: edges and middle
bullets: Leukocytes are not spread evenly: larger cells (granulocytes, monocytes) gather at the edges and tail, lymphocytes nearer the middle. Counting only the middle or only the edge distorts the differential.
The former-USSR textbook method: move in a zigzag (meander) covering edges and middle, or in cross-wise tracks from edge to middle at several places; never repeat a field.
Former-USSR textbooks usually count 200 leukocytes and halve each number to get a percentage; the WHO manual counts 100 cells. Your laboratory SOP decides which.

slides.title: No counter: a paper tally table
bullets: 1. Draw columns N, E, B, L, M on paper (separate columns for bands and segmented cells if your report lists them) and 10 rows.
2. Put one stroke in the right column for each cell; after 10 strokes in a row move to the next row.
3. Ten rows filled means 100 cells: each column total equals the percentage (for 200 cells use 20 rows and halve the totals).
4. In SI units write the fraction as a decimal: 59 → 0.59; absolute count = fraction × WBC.

slides.title: Staining faults and fixes
bullets: Too blue — the water is alkaline. Too red — it is acidic. Make neutral water fresh: it turns acidic in air.
If too blue: rinse twice in 1% boric acid in 95% ethanol, then wash at once in neutral water. Next time use a slightly more acidic buffer.
Little black dots are stain deposit. Wash glassware daily (no acid) and filter the stain.
May–Grünwald deposit: rinse twice in methanol, dry and re-stain with fresh or filtered stain.
Giemsa deposit: rinse with methanol, wash at once in neutral water and repeat the staining.
Dye impurities also spoil staining — a standardized stain is recommended.

slides.title: Other smear artefacts
bullets: Leukocyte clumps: usually with infection (neutrophils) or lymphoproliferative disorders (lymphocytes); falsely lower the analyser WBC and hamper the differential.
Damaged granulocytes and fuzzy-looking red cells may suggest hyperlipidaemia.
Smudge cells are remnants of broken leukocytes; see “Cells”.

slides.title: Peripheral blood smear
slides.caption:
White blood cell at the centre (neutrophil): white cells are typically seen in a peripheral blood smear. Neutrophils are a type of white cell and one of the body's main defences against infection; finding them in a smear is normal. Numerous red blood cells: they carry oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and return carbon dioxide to the lungs. Many red cells in a smear are normal; a high number may be linked to polycythaemia or dehydration. Platelets (dot-like bodies): small cell fragments involved in clotting and wound healing, seen as small dots. A normal platelet number is essential for clotting; low counts (thrombocytopenia) or abnormal function can cause bleeding disorders.

slides.title: Reference values and decision limits
slides.footnote: The reference interval varies by laboratory, method and population; the laboratory verifies its own interval (verification).

slides.title: Which of these, per the source, causes a LOW white count (leukopenia)?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: HIV attacks white cells and causes leukopenia.

Basis: HIV, bone marrow damage, cancers affecting the marrow and lupus cause leukopenia; infection and burns cause leukocytosis.

slides.title: The WBC is above normal. Does that alone confirm a diagnosis?
options: Yes, a high count confirms an infection
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: it is read with a differential, smear and other tests.

Basis: A WBC shows whether the count is high or low but cannot confirm a diagnosis.

slides.title: What does the term “neutropenia” mean?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Too many neutrophils is neutrophilia; too few is neutropenia.

slides.title: Why does a patient on chemotherapy have regular blood tests (NCI)?
options: Because chemotherapy raises platelets too much
Only to follow the sedimentation rate
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct: low neutrophils raise the risk of infection.

Basis: At times in the cycle neutrophils are particularly low and infection risk rises.

slides.title: Which two main types make up lymphocytes?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: Lymphocytes are B cells and T cells.

slides.title: Which test does the source name for checking the immune system in HIV?
slides.explanation:
Explanation: Correct.

Basis: HIV destroys CD4 cells, which are counted by a separate test.

slides.title: In acute leukemia, the peripheral blood shows:
Which cells of the granulocytic lineage normally enter the peripheral blood:
options: Band and segmented neutrophils, eosinophils, basophils

slides.title: Which method is more effective for determining the type of acute leukemia:
options: trephine biopsy of the iliac bone
slides.explanation: Explanation: Among the options, cytochemistry is the most correct; the current standard is flow cytometry (immunophenotyping).

slides.title: What is a leukocyte left shift:
options: appearance of degeneratively changed leukocytes in the blood
appearance of immature leukocytes in peripheral blood (increase of band cells, metamyelocytes and myeloblasts)
increase of only band cells in the blood
appearance of only segmented leukocytes in the blood

slides.title: Blood picture more characteristic of chronic myeloid leukemia:
options: hyperleukocytosis, granulocytosis with left shift down to myelocytes

slides.title: Most informative in determining the variant of acute leukemia:
options: trephine biopsy of the pelvic bone

slides.title: Counting the leukocyte differential?
bullets: 1. The differential is the percentage ratio of leukocyte types; manually, 100 (preferably 200) cells are counted under oil immersion in a smear stained by Romanowsky, then absolute counts are calculated (percentage × WBC).

2. Smear quality: thin, with a "tail", evenly distributed; counting along a path covering the edge and middle parts of the smear (cells are distributed unevenly – large cells are more numerous at the edges).
3. Normal (adults): neutrophils 40–60%, lymphocytes 20–40%, monocytes 2–8%, eosinophils 0–4%, basophils 0.5–1%; interpretation is based on absolute counts.

4. Automated differential (5 populations) on the analyzer; with an abnormal result, a "flag" or suspected blasts, a smear is examined manually. The uncertainty of manual counting is especially large for rare cells (blasts, immature granulocytes).

slides.title: Counting the leukocyte differential?
bullets: 5. Interpretation: neutrophilia and a "left shift" (increase in bands) – bacterial infection/stress; lymphocytosis – viral infections, CLL; eosinophilia – allergy, parasites; monocytosis – chronic infections; basophilia – myeloproliferative diseases.

slides.title: Leukemoid reactions of myeloid, lymphomonocytic and eosinophilic type?
bullets: 1. A leukemoid reaction is a reactive (non-neoplastic) blood change resembling leukemia; in the myeloid type neutrophils are usually >50×10⁹/L, mainly mature forms, with no myeloproliferative neoplasm.
2. Causes of the myeloid type: severe bacterial infections, sepsis, hemorrhage, hemolysis, tumors (paraneoplastic), drugs (glucocorticoids, G-CSF), intoxications.

3. Difference from CML: in a leukemoid reaction basophilia and blasts are usually absent, leukocyte alkaline phosphatase (LAP) is high, BCR::ABL1 (Philadelphia) is negative, polyclonal; it normalizes after the underlying cause is removed.
4. Lymphocytic (lymphomonocytic) type: viral infections (EBV, CMV), whooping cough, etc. – lymphocytosis, atypical (reactive) lymphocytes; to distinguish from CLL – flow cytometry (clonality).

slides.title: Leukemoid reactions of myeloid, lymphomonocytic and eosinophilic type?
bullets: 5. Eosinophilic type: eosinophils >0.5×10⁹/L, sometimes very high – allergy, helminth infestations, drug reactions, rheumatological diseases; exclude clonal eosinophilic neoplasms.

slides.title: Leukocyte differential, leukocytosis, leukopenia?
bullets: 1. The differential is the ratio of leukocyte types (%), always interpreted together with absolute counts; determined manually on a smear or on an analyzer.

2. Leukocytosis – in adults >11×10⁹/L; physiological (stress, exertion, pregnancy) and pathological (infections, inflammation, necrosis, leukemias, drugs – glucocorticoids). Types: neutrophilia, lymphocytosis, monocytosis, eosinophilia (>0.5×10⁹/L), basophilia.
3. Leukemoid reaction – neutrophils >50×10⁹/L without a myeloproliferative disease; hyperleukocytosis – >100×10⁹/L (usually leukemia).

4. Causes of leukopenia (mainly neutropenia): viral infections, some bacterial infections, drugs and chemotherapy (myelotoxic), autoimmune, B12/folate deficiency, bone marrow aplasia or infiltration, hypersplenism; agranulocytosis – a sharp decrease of granulocytes, risk of severe infection.

slides.title: Leukocyte differential, leukocytosis, leukopenia?
bullets: 5. Morphological changes: "left shift" (bands and immature forms), toxic granulation; hypersegmentation – a sign of megaloblastic anemia; blasts – suspicion of leukemia, smear and hematologist consultation.
